newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvian PM says balanced budget means "new life".
newsitem.headline: Latvian PM says balanced budget means "new life".

text.p: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Shkele said on Wednesday that parliament's backing for a balanced 1997 budget would breathe new life into the economy of the small Baltic state.
Parliament earlier passed Latvia's first deficit-free budget, which would come after a planned 40 million lat deficit in 1996 and a 90 million lat deficit in 1995.
"It is the start of a new life for Latvia," Shkele told Reuters in an interview after the vote.
He said the balanced budget would free up resources to spend on helping to expand economy rather than paying interest on government securities.
Latvia, which quit the former Soviet Union in 1991, has had a troubled path in following market reforms.
It seemed set for growth of some three percent in 1995 when it was hit by what turned out to be one of eastern Europe's worst banking crises.
The crisis was caused by the closure of its largest bank, Banka Baltiya, and thousands of people lost their savings.
It caused several other banks to close and the economy to shrink by just under one percent.

Shkele, a non-party businessman brought in as prime minister expressly to help bring economic order, has stressed the balanced budget as a key tool in bringing down inflation and interest rates and stimulating the economy as a whole.
"This will help stabilise the system and bring down inflation," Shkele said.
He said that annual inflation in 1996 could be around 13 percent and may be in single figures next year.
Inflation in November was an annual 14.4 percent compared to 1995 annual inflation of 23.1 percent.
Growth of around one percent is expected this year rising to two or three percent in 1997.
Shkele said the main task now was to make sure the balanced budget was actually fulfilled.

The deficit-free budget has been controversial as teachers, health workers and others in state-funded areas say too large sacrifices are being made in a country where many are still forced to live on very litte.
